title: Rav Geviha of Bei Katil
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: Hyman infers that apparently he was Rava’s student, as in Avodah Zarah 22a, where he relates an incident that took place before Rava, as an eyewitness. Hyman states that in Ameimar’s time he was already the leading sage of the generation, as in Beitzah 23a, where he expounded at the Exilarch’s gate, and Ameimar and Rav Ashi discussed his ruling.

Hyman describes how, when Rav Ashi founded his great academy in Mata Mechasya, Rav Geviha took a large part in arranging the Talmud, as we find in Yevamot 60a and Chullin 26b: “Rav Geviha of Bei Katil went and told the teaching before Rav Ashi.” He likewise always raised difficulties against Rav Ashi as colleague to colleague, as in Bava Batra 83a, Menachot 8a, Chullin 64b and Me’ilah 10a.

He is likewise mentioned in Bava Kamma 82a. According to Rav Sherira Gaon in his Epistle, part 3, chapter 3, he headed the academy in Pumbedita from the year 730, after the death of Rav Acha son of Rava, until the year 744, and after him Rafram headed it.

notes.text: The apparent Rava studentship, academy role and always-as-colleague claim are Hyman’s inferences. The academy years תשל/תשמד are retained as730/744 without an invented era or conversion.

The leading-generation assertion, Talmud-arrangement role and always-as-colleague argument are Hyman’s. The consulted Avodah Zarah 22a records a Rava incident under the name Geviha of Bei Khetil; that alone does not establish studentship, academy leadership or a dated era.
